paper_metadata.title: Quantum Quantile Mechanics: Solving Stochastic Diﬀerential Equations for Generating Time-Series

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based quantum quantile mechanics (QQM) method for stochastic differential equations and benchmarks it on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process using 6 qubits, 6-layer HEA circuits, and noiseless statevector simulation in Yao.jl. It also studies a continuous qGAN on the same target with 2000 training epochs, finding that QQM produces better-behaved quantile functions and sampling than the reordered qGAN generator, but no practical quantum advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Quantum quantile mechanics (QQM) training of a differentiable quantum circuit to represent and time-evolve the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck quantile function from an analytic initial condition, followed by sampling and comparison to Euler-Maruyama.

algorithm.variant: quantum quantile mechanics with differentiable quantum circuits (DQC) and quantile-mechanics time propagation
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA) with six layers of generic single-qubit rotations plus nearest-neighbor CNOTs
algorithm.convergence_criteria: fixed number of epochs; training loss reported to converge rapidly

hyperparameters.shots: expectation-value based readout; multiple shots required (exact number not reported)

problem_formulation.encoding_details: latent variable z and time t are encoded via product feature maps using arcsin rotations on each qubit; output is an expectation-value readout of a variational circuit representing the quantile function
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize data loss plus SDE differential loss so that G(z,t) satisfies the quantilized Fokker-Planck equation for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: differential constraint via quantile-mechanics PDE loss; floating boundary handling for the initial condition

problem_instance.description: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic process used as a benchmark for financial forecasting/trading and time-series generation

dataset_specification.description: analytic initial delta distribution evolved to Gaussian; parameters nu=1, sigma=0.7, x0=4, t0=-0.2

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: none reported beyond analytic initial condition and uniform latent sampling
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: compare generated histograms against analytic PDF and Euler-Maruyama samples at Tmin, Tmid, Tmax; 100,000 samples used for histogram comparison

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; Euler-Maruyama used only as classical baseline
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: histogram binning and normalization of 100,000 samples

speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic or empirical speedup is reported; the paper emphasizes NISQ suitability and sampling utility.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not enough complexity data; paper reports a 6-qubit noiseless statevector simulation only.
limiting_factors: No hardware execution on a QPU
No asymptotic complexity or crossover analysis

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states a full quantum state simulator in a noiseless setting implemented in Yao.jl and no QPU is named.
Speedup order set to none_proven because the paper discusses practical NISQ suitability but does not provide an asymptotic quantum speedup claim.
The paper benchmarks against Euler-Maruyama for sample quality, but does not claim or demonstrate computational advantage.

experiments.description: Quantum quantile learning from data for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process at the initial time, followed by QQM time propagation and sampling.

algorithm.variant: quantum circuit learning (QCL) of the initial quantile function, then quantum quantile mechanics propagation
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient ansatz (same six-qubit variational circuit as the QQM experiment)
algorithm.convergence_criteria: fixed number of epochs; target loss around 10^-6

hyperparameters.feature_map: tower-type product feature map U_phi'(z)=⊗_j exp[-i arcsin(z) j Z_j/2]
hyperparameters.initialization: pre-training with product states can reduce epochs; optional initialization layers discussed in supplement
hyperparameters.shots: expectation-value based readout; multiple shots required (exact number not reported)

algorithm.parameter_initialization: pre-training with product states; optional classical initialization of variational parameters from low-order regression is discussed in supplement

problem_formulation.encoding_details: sorted samples from the initial distribution are mapped to latent variable points in [-1,1] and fit by a quantum circuit representing the quantile function
problem_formulation.objective_function: fit the initial quantile function from observed samples, then enforce quantile-mechanics evolution in time
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: data fitting plus differential constraint from the quantile-mechanics PDE

problem_instance.description: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with data-inferred initial condition

dataset_specification.description: 100,000 ordered samples from the initial distribution; 43 Chebyshev training points used

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: samples binned, sorted in ascending order, and interpolated; Chebyshev points emphasize tails
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: compare learned initial quantile to analytic target; sample histograms at initial and later times; 100,000 samples for histogram evaluation

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; classical regression used only for optional initialization; Euler-Maruyama used as baseline for propagated samples
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: sorting and binning of samples; interpolation to target quantile values
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: histogram binning and normalization of 100,000 samples

speedup_claims.caveats: No speedup claim is made; the paper highlights data-frugal training and good sampling quality.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not enough complexity data; paper reports 6 qubits, 43 training points, and noiseless simulation only.
limiting_factors: No hardware execution on a QPU
Classical baseline used only for comparison, not advantage demonstration

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states implementation in a full quantum state simulator with Yao.jl and no physical device.
Speedup order set to none_proven because the paper emphasizes data-frugal training and NISQ suitability, not asymptotic speedup.
The paper shows good sample fidelity for learned quantiles, but no advantage over classical methods is established.

experiments.description: Continuous qGAN training on the same Ornstein-Uhlenbeck target distribution, including generator/discriminator training and reordered-quantile analysis.

algorithm.variant: continuous qGAN / variational quantum generator for continuous distributions
algorithm.ansatz: expressive Chebyshev tower feature map followed by 6-layer HEA for both generator and discriminator
algorithm.convergence_criteria: train for 2000 epochs; select best generator when generator and discriminator losses are within 0.1 and KS distance is minimal

hyperparameters.target_distribution: normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.2

algorithm.parameter_initialization: optimal circuit parameters saved when losses briefly settle near Nash equilibrium; no explicit initial parameter distribution reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: latent variable z in [-1,1] is embedded by a feature map; generator outputs a continuous sample via expectation value
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimax GAN objective to match the target continuous distribution
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: adversarial discriminator training; best model selected by KS test rather than direct loss minimization

problem_instance.description: Learning a continuous normal distribution as a proxy for the OU initial distribution and analyzing the generator as a reordered quantile function
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: train for 2000 epochs; compare generated histogram to target PDF; choose best generator by KS test when losses are close to Nash equilibrium

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; Kolmogorov-Smirnov test used for model selection
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: histogram binning and normalization of 100,000 samples; reordering of generator outputs into a monotone quantile function for analysis

speedup_claims.caveats: No speedup claim is reported; qGAN is discussed as a continuous generative model and its limitations are emphasized.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not enough complexity data; the qGAN is trained in simulation for 2000 epochs on a 6-qubit circuit.
limiting_factors: No hardware execution on a QPU
Training is oscillatory and only approximate
No advantage over classical generative modeling is demonstrated

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the qGAN is presented with the same numerical simulation setup and no physical QPU is named.
Speedup order set to none_proven because the paper argues about trainability and quantile structure, not asymptotic quantum advantage.
The paper explicitly notes qGAN generators are less suitable for time propagation and do not outperform the QQM approach.
